text: At one in the morning, gold miners in the Rocky Mountains got up and started making breakfast.
The sky was so bright, they thought the Sun had risen.
That same night, telegraph wires threw sparks. Operators got electric shocks. In some offices, the paper caught fire.
It was September 1859. And the Sun had just hit the Earth with the biggest storm we have ever recorded.
In 2012, it fired another one just as big. It missed us by about a week.
This is the story of the storm that already happened — and what it would do to a world that now runs on electricity.
On the morning of the first of September, an English astronomer named Richard Carrington was drawing sunspots.
He pointed his telescope at the Sun and projected its image onto a sheet of paper — the safe way to look at it.
At eleven eighteen, two beads of blinding white light burst out of a group of sunspots.
He ran to find a witness. By the time he got back, a minute later, the light was already fading. Five minutes — and it was gone.
Carrington had seen the first solar flare in history.
What he couldn't see was the cloud it launched: billions of tonnes of magnetised gas, flying towards the Earth.
Storms like that usually take two or three days to cross. This one took seventeen and a half hours.

section: II. The night the sky caught fire (1:40–2:40)
text: When it hit, the Earth's magnetic field shook like a bell.

section: II. The night the sky caught fire (1:40–2:40)
text: Auroras — the northern lights — were seen over Cuba, over Jamaica, over Hawaii.

section: II. The night the sky caught fire (1:40–2:40)
text: In the north-eastern United States, people read their newspapers outside, at midnight, by the light of the sky.

section: II. The night the sky caught fire (1:40–2:40)
text: But the strangest thing happened on the wires.

section: II. The night the sky caught fire (1:40–2:40)
text: The storm pushed electric currents into every long metal line on Earth. And in 1859, the longest metal lines were telegraph wires.

section: II. The night the sky caught fire (1:40–2:40)
text: Between Boston and Portland, the operators unplugged their batteries completely — and kept sending messages for two hours, powered by the sky.

section: II. The night the sky caught fire (1:40–2:40)
text: In 1859 that was a curiosity. Today, we have wrapped the whole planet in metal lines.

section: III. What a storm does now (2:40–3:45)
text: We don't have to guess. Smaller storms have already shown us.

section: III. What a storm does now (2:40–3:45)
text: In March 1989, a storm hit Quebec. The power grid collapsed in about ninety seconds. Six million people lost electricity.

section: III. What a storm does now (2:40–3:45)
text: In 1972, a storm set off dozens of American sea mines off the coast of Vietnam. Nobody touched them. The magnetic field did.

section: III. What a storm does now (2:40–3:45)
text: In 2022, SpaceX launched forty-nine Starlink satellites into a minor storm. It puffed up the atmosphere, and dragged thirty-eight of them back down to burn.

section: III. What a storm does now (2:40–3:45)
text: And in May 2024, in the middle of planting season, farm tractors across the American Midwest lost their GPS and stopped steering themselves.

section: III. What a storm does now (2:40–3:45)
text: None of these were Carrington-sized. Not even close.
On the twenty-third of July 2012, the Sun fired a cloud that was.
A NASA spacecraft called STEREO happened to be in its path, and measured it. It was as fast as 1859. Maybe faster.
It crossed the Earth's orbit where we had been about a week earlier.
A report for the US National Academies estimated what a direct hit could cost: up to two trillion dollars in the first year — and four to ten years to recover.
The weakest point is the giant transformers that run the grid. Burn enough of them, and there are no spares. Each one is built to order, and takes a year or more to make.
Today, we're not drawing sunspots on paper.
Spacecraft watch the Sun all day, every day. When a cloud leaves it, we know within hours — and get one to three days' warning.
And a probe parked a million and a half kilometres towards the Sun gives us the final alarm: somewhere between fifteen minutes and an hour.
Enough to put satellites to sleep, reroute flights away from the poles, and ease the load on the grid.
So how likely is another Carrington?
One study put it at about twelve percent per decade. Later ones say closer to one or two.
Nobody knows the last digit. We only know it isn't zero.
Somewhere on the Sun, the next one is already waiting. This time, we'll see it coming.
